fixes.explanation: Right, baker. The text says the field, the cave, "and all the trees within the boundaries of the field were deeded over to Abraham's possession" in front of the Hittites at the gate (Genesis 23:17-18). So the trees are part of the package. That's like buying the whole batch and getting every last crumb in the bag. Then Abraham buries his wife Sarah in that cave (Genesis 23:19).

That's it, baker. Sarah dies in Kiriath-arba, which is Hebron, and "…Abraham went out to mourn and to weep for her." (Genesis 23:2) The text gives us mourning and weeping, plain and simple. I think a man who loses his wife is allowed every one of those tears.

I get why you'd think so, since Isaac is Abraham's son (Genesis 21:3). But this passage never says Abraham sends word to anybody. What it says is that he "…went out to mourn and to weep for her." (Genesis 23:2) Sometimes the story just stops and lets a man cry.

Right on the money, baker. Abraham says, "Give me a burial site among you so that I can bury my dead." (Genesis 23:4) He opens by calling himself a foreigner and an outsider among them. Then he makes his request: a burial site.

Close to the sort of thing a traveler might ask for, friend, but not what he says here. Abraham asks for a burial site, not grazing land (Genesis 23:4). His words are about burying his dead. Sheep don't come up in this request at all.

Good guess if you were picturing a man at a market, friend. But his actual request is for a burial site (Genesis 23:4). He says he wants it "…so that I can bury my dead." Setting up shop isn't what he asks for.

Not here, friend. Abraham doesn't turn them down. He rises, bows down, and then asks them to approach Ephron son of Zohar on his behalf (Genesis 23:7-8). He asks for their help right there in the same breath.

Nope, he stays put. After the Hittites offer him their finest tombs (Genesis 23:6), the text says he rose and bowed down before them (Genesis 23:7). Then he keeps talking with them about the cave of Machpelah (Genesis 23:8-9). Nobody in this scene is heading off to look anywhere else.

No waiting in this scene, friend. Ephron's answer is, "I give you the field, and I give you the cave that is in it." (Genesis 23:11) He says it with all the Hittites at the city gate listening. Nothing in his words asks Abraham to hold on.

Yes, baker. Ephron says he gives the field and the cave (Genesis 23:11), and Abraham answers, "…I will pay you the price of the field. Accept it from me, so that I may bury my dead there." (Genesis 23:13) He bows again before the people of the land and asks to pay. Gift offered, payment requested. That's quite a moment.

Careful, baker, that one slipped past. The text says Ephron's field, the cave, "and all the trees within the boundaries of the field were deeded over to Abraham's possession." (Genesis 23:17-18) So the trees growing within that field's boundaries go to Abraham too. They're part of the deal, not left behind.
